text.p: $PNAME supports ThreadX in two ways, either using Percepio's TraceRecorder library (recommended) or using the tx_trace library included in ThreadX and described in this section.

The recommended ThreadX integration using the Percepio TraceRecorder library allows for both snapshots and streaming trace, while the tx_trace library described here is limited to snapshots from a ring-buffer.

The ThreadX tx_trace library monitors not only the core ThreadX kernel, but also the NetX, UsbX and FileX middleware stacks. All such events can be analyzed with $PRODUCT, as well as User Events that allow for custom logging in the system.
text.note: The tx_trace library does not always provide the status of API calls, which affects the $PNAME functionality. Errors or timeout (orange labels) are only shown in some special cases (like tx_byte_allocate). For other API functions, white or green labels are no guarantee that the call succeeded. You may however insert User Events to log relevant error codes returned by the API calls. Consider using the TraceRecorder integration instead of the tx_trace library.

text.p: Some applications use an explicit idle thread (or one per core on SMP systems). If present, $PNAME has to detect these in order to meaningfully calculate CPU load. When loading tx_trace traces (.trx files), $PNAME uses the thread name and scheduling priority to recognize idle threads. It assumes that any thread using priority 31 is an idle thread, regardless of TX_MAX_PRIORITIES. If the wrong thread is recognized as idle, the trace might not load or display properly. Please check the following before using $PNAME with tx_trace traces:

ul.li: When you have an idle thread in your system, make sure that either its name contains the word "idle" in any casing, or that its priority is 31.
Check that the word "idle" (in any casing) is not used in names of regular (non-idle) threads. For example, "briDleTask" would be incorrectly matched as an idle thread.
Ensure that priority 31 is not used by regular (non-idle) threads.

text.p: To view the trace in $PNAME, you need to save a binary dump of the trace buffer (the one specified for tx_trace_enable) to a host-side file named "<file name>.trx", that you open in $PNAME. The data should be in binary or Intel Hex format.
You can easily configure IAR Embedded Workbench and e2 studio to save the trace and also open it in $PNAME, as described below. Similar integrations are also possible using other IDEs.

To enable quick access to $PNAME and the current trace, you may include $PNAME in the Tools menu, with "trace.trx" specified as parameter.
Select "Configure Tools..." in the Tools menu
Add a new entry "$PNAME"
Set the path to the $PNAME executable (the ".exe" file).
Set the argument to "$$PROJ_DIR$$\trace.trx"
This will open $PNAME and load the provided trace file.
$PNAME can utilize the same e2 studio integration as the legacy tool TraceX.

To configure e2 studio to use $PNAME as trace viewer, go to Window -> Preferences -> Renesas -> TraceX, and enter the path to $PNAME instead of the legacy TraceX tool. On Windows, the default path is: C:\Program Files\Percepio\Tracealyzer 4\Tracealyzer.exe

Then, to upload the trace from e2 studio, select Run -> TraceX -> Launch TraceX Debugging. Enter the address of the trace buffer (e.g. "&g_tx_trace_buffer") and the size ("sizeof(g_tx_trace_buffer)"). Click OK. Now e2 studio will save the trace buffer into a file and open it with $PNAME.

The ThreadX recorder assigns a high-resolution timestamp to each event, but it does not report the "timestamp frequency", i.e., the clock frequency of the time source. So, to get an accurate time scale in $PNAME, you need to specify the timestamp frequency in File -> Settings -> Timestamp Frequency.

This setting should reflect how frequently the time source is updated. Depending on your ThreadX port, the timestamp frequency is often the processor's core clock frequency. For instance, if using a Renesas Synergy S7G2 processor at 240 Mhz, you should enter 240000000. After updating the timestamp frequency, you need to reload the trace for the setting to take effect.

Custom Timestamping
The ThreadX timestamping is defined by these two macros in tx_port.h. In case you want to use a custom time source for the tracing, you can override these definitions, e.g., in tx_user.h.

ul.li: TX_TRACE_TIME_SOURCE: How to read the current time (i.e., the time source).
TX_TRACE_TIME_MASK: A bit mask applied to the timestamp (e.g., 0x00FFFFFFUL for a 24-bit timer).

text.p: The ThreadX tx_trace library allows for inserting your own custom events, called User Events. This allows you may trace and visualize any event or data in your firmware in several different ways, including data plots, custom intervals and state graphs. You may also apply the Event Interpretation feature to change how the events are displayed.
User Events are added by calling tx_trace_user_event_insert.

pre.code: UINT tx_trace_user_event_insert(ULONG event_id, ULONG info_field_1, ULONG info_field_2, ULONG info_field_3, ULONG info_field_4)

text.p: The parameter event_id is a numeric code that you assign as a unique identifier for this event, in the range TX_TRACE_USER_EVENT_START (4096) to TX_TRACE_USER_EVENT_END (65535). The "info_field" parameters allow for logging up to four 32-bit integer values in a single timestamped event.

User Event are saved quickly and can usually be used also in time-critical code without adding significant overhead. If taking ARM Cortex-M MCUs as example, a User Event takes about 100-200 clock cycles depending on compiler and optimization level. That is often less than 1 microsecond.

Possible return values from tx_trace_user_event_insert are:
TX_SUCCESS (0x00): The user event was logged correctly.
TX_NOT_DONE (0x20): If the tracing has not been enabled correctly using tx_trace_enable.
TX_FEATURE_NOT_ENABLED (0xFF): Returned if event tracing is not enabled in the build (see TX_ENABLE_EVENT_TRACE above).
To trace Interrupt Service Routines, you need to add calls to tx_trace_isr_enter_insert and tx_trace_isr_exit_insert in each handler function you wish to trace.
Call tx_trace_isr_enter_insert in the very beginning of the ISRs you want to trace.
Each call to "isr_enter" call should have a matching "isr_exit" call, in the very end of the traced ISR.
The parameter isr_id is the identifier displayed in $PNAME. For instance, if isr_id is 1, $PNAME will label this execution as "ISR1".

The ThreadX function tx_trace_enable() should be called in order to initialize and activate the event tracing.
UINT tx_trace_enable(VOID* trace_buffer_start, ULONG trace_buffer_size, ULONG registry_entries)

Where the parameters are:
trace_buffer_start: Pointer to a buffer for the recorded events, allocated by the user.
trace_buffer_size: The size of the buffer, in bytes.
registry_entries: The number of ThreadX objects to keep in the trace registry. This allows for displaying object names, instead of just addresses.

Make sure to check the return values from tx_trace_enable. They are:
TX_SUCCESS (0x00): Tracing was enabled correctly.
TX_SIZE_ERROR (0x05): The provided buffer was too small.
TX_NOT_DONE (0x20): Returned if tx_trace_enable has already been called.
TX_FEATURE_NOT_ENABLED (0xFF): Returned if event tracing is not enabled in the build (see TX_ENABLE_EVENT_TRACE above).
Assuming that the return value is TX_SUCCESS, the event tracing is now active. The event data can be extracted from target RAM whenever suitable.
